lead: This unit explains how a vehicle stores, generates, controls and distributes electrical energy for cranking and running. After it, the student can read a charging or starting circuit, choose battery and alternator ratings for a load, and explain starter control and power distribution in exam language.
about: This unit follows the electrical path from battery to starter and alternator. Chapter 1.1 maps how vehicle electronics grew from ignition and lighting to networked control. Chapters 1.2 and 1.3 open the lead-acid battery: construction, chemical action, ratings, tests and maintenance-free types. Chapter 1.4 traces the charging circuit, then 1.5 and 1.6 explain the alternator, its curves, losses and voltage regulation. Chapters 1.7 and 1.8 cover what an IC engine needs for cranking and how starter motors, drives and control circuits meet that need. Chapter 1.9 closes with high-voltage circuits and vehicle power distribution, linking the 12 V backbone to ignition secondary and, briefly, EV traction supply.

chapters.idea: Vehicle electronics evolved from simple ignition and lighting loads to networked control because emission, safety and comfort demands grew.
chapters.depth: Cover a cause-and-effect chain: hand crank and magneto; battery-coil ignition; 6 V to 12 V; dynamo to alternator; mechanical to electronic ignition; carburettor to EFI and ECU; separate wires to CAN buses; driver assistance and electrified traction. Add a one-page system map naming engine block, cylinder head, piston, crankshaft, camshaft, connecting rod, valve, four-stroke cycle, drivetrain, transmission, drive shaft, differential, suspension, brakes and steering only as parts that electrical systems serve; no mechanical design calculations. Mention Euro I–V and equivalent Bharat Stage laws as drivers; keep limits and test cycles for Unit 4. Some syllabi call this 'electronics in automotive and its evolution'.

figure.title: Evolution chain
figure.aria: A downward chain from hand crank to CAN and ADAS shows how vehicle electrical systems grew into networked electronic control.

chapters.example: A 1970 car has a 35 A dynamo; a 2020 car has a 120 A alternator. Both are regulated at 14.0 V. Compare the maximum electrical power available. Answer: 35 A × 14.0 V = 490 W; 120 A × 14.0 V = 1680 W; the increase is 1190 W, about 3.4 times.
chapters.trap: The evolution is not only entertainment; emission laws and safety pushed electronic control. Do not date every step or treat Bharat Stage as a separate physics from Euro norms.
chapters.prereq: Basic DC circuits from first-year physics.
chapters.leave: Detailed emission limits to Unit 4; ignition and lighting to Unit 2; sensors and actuators to Unit 3; network protocols to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A lead-acid cell stores energy in two lead-based plates and dilute sulfuric acid, and six cells give the 12 V battery.
chapters.depth: Cover construction: positive plate of lead dioxide (PbO₂) on a grid, negative plate of spongy lead (Pb), separators, dilute sulfuric acid electrolyte of about 1.26–1.28 specific gravity, container, terminals and vents. Name Plante and pasted plates. Explain discharge and charge reactions at both plates and the overall cell reaction; define cell voltage about 2.1 V, gassing, sulfation, stratification and self-discharge. Distinguish battery from cell. Keep rating tests for Chapter 3.

figure.aria: A cell stack shows a negative lead plate, a separator, a positive lead dioxide plate and dilute sulfuric acid electrolyte, with six such cells giving about 12.6 V.

chapters.example: A 12 V lead-acid battery has six cells. A fully charged cell has an open-circuit voltage of 2.1 V. Find the battery voltage. If one cell is shorted, find the new voltage. Answer: 6 × 2.1 V = 12.6 V; 5 × 2.1 V = 10.5 V.
chapters.trap: The positive plate is PbO₂ and the negative plate is Pb, not the reverse. A 12 V battery has six cells, and each cell is about 2.1 V, not 2.0 V.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 for the battery's role; basic oxidation and reduction from chemistry.
chapters.leave: Ratings, testing and sealed types to Chapter 3; charging voltage to Chapter 4; battery sensing to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Ratings such as Ah, CCA and reserve capacity state what a battery can store and deliver, while tests reveal its real health.
chapters.depth: Define ampere-hour (Ah) at the 20 h rate, reserve capacity in minutes at 25 A to 10.5 V, cold cranking amps (CCA at −18 °C for 30 s to 7.2 V) and cranking amps. Cover hydrometer specific gravity, open-circuit voltage, load test, conductance test and charging-system test, with safety precautions. Explain maintenance-free designs: calcium grids, sealed VRLA, absorbent glass mat (AGM), gas recombination and enhanced flooded battery (EFB) for start-stop. Some syllabi call this battery ratings and testing.

figure.aria: Two discharge curves show a weak battery falling below 10.5 V earlier than a good battery under the same load.

chapters.example: A battery is rated 60 Ah at the 20 h rate. Find the constant current for the 20 h test. If it delivers 45 Ah before reaching 10.5 V, find the capacity retained as a percentage. Answer: 60 Ah ÷ 20 h = 3 A; 45/60 × 100 = 75%.
chapters.trap: Ah is stored charge, not starting current. CCA is measured at −18 °C, not at room temperature, and reserve capacity is in minutes, not Ah.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2 for cell construction and discharge.
chapters.leave: State-of-charge sensing to Unit 3; charging circuit to Chapter 4; start-stop control to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: The charging system turns engine rotation into a regulated DC bus voltage that runs loads and restores the battery.
chapters.depth: Cover components: battery, alternator, rectifier, voltage regulator, warning lamp, ignition switch, fuses and grounds. Draw and label a charging circuit with B+ (battery positive), B− (battery negative), D+ (field or excitation) and L (lamp) terminals, plus voltage sense. Explain initial excitation through the warning lamp, field current control, charging voltage about 13.8–14.4 V and temperature dependence. Show current paths at low and high load. Keep alternator construction for Chapter 5 and regulator circuits for Chapter 6.

figure.title: Charging circuit
figure.aria: A charging block diagram runs from engine belt to alternator, rectifier and DC bus, with the regulator sensing bus voltage and controlling alternator field current.

chapters.example: A car alternator is regulated at 14.2 V. The battery open-circuit voltage is 12.4 V and its internal resistance is 0.02 Ω. Neglect wiring resistance. Find the initial charging current. Answer: I = (14.2 − 12.4) V ÷ 0.02 Ω = 1.8 V ÷ 0.02 Ω = 90 A. The current falls as the battery charges.
chapters.trap: The regulator controls field current; it does not raise voltage by increasing engine speed. The warning lamp often provides initial field excitation, so a dead bulb can stop charging.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2 and 3 for battery voltage and capacity; basic AC rectification.
chapters.leave: Alternator construction and curves to Chapter 5; regulator types to Chapter 6; battery current sensing to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: An alternator makes three-phase AC by rotating a field winding inside stator coils, and a diode bridge rectifies it to DC.
chapters.depth: Cover Faraday's law, three-phase stator, claw-pole rotor with field winding, slip rings and brushes, rectifier bridge, fan and housing. Explain cut-in speed, rated output current, pulley ratio and ripple. Draw and interpret characteristic curves of output current against speed at constant regulated voltage, and voltage against speed. Some syllabi call this alternator versions and generation of electrical energy in the vehicle.

figure.aria: Output current rises steeply at low speed and levels off near the rated current as alternator speed increases.

chapters.example: An alternator has 12 poles and runs at 6000 rpm. Find the frequency of the stator AC before rectification. Answer: f = (p × N) ÷ 120 = (12 × 6000) ÷ 120 = 600 Hz.
chapters.trap: The alternator generates AC; the diodes make DC. Output current does not rise forever with speed because the regulator limits field current. Do not confuse engine rpm with alternator rpm when a pulley ratio is given.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4 for the charging circuit; basic three-phase AC and diodes.
chapters.leave: Losses and voltage regulation to Chapter 6; ignition high voltage to Chapter 9; charging control in the ECU to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Alternator efficiency falls because of copper, iron, diode and mechanical losses, and the voltage regulator balances field current to hold the bus voltage.
chapters.depth: Cover losses: stator and field copper loss (I²R), core iron loss from hysteresis and eddy currents, rectifier diode forward loss (two diodes conduct), brush and slip-ring loss, bearing and fan windage. Use power balance P_in = P_out + losses and efficiency η = P_out ÷ P_in × 100. Explain electromechanical and electronic voltage regulators, voltage sensing, field PWM, temperature compensation, load response and overvoltage protection. Some syllabi call this power losses and voltage regulations versions.

figure.aria: A power tree splits alternator input into useful output and copper, iron, diode and mechanical loss paths.

chapters.example: An alternator delivers 14.0 V at 70 A. Its input mechanical power is 1.30 kW. Find output power and efficiency. Answer: P_out = 14.0 V × 70 A = 980 W; η = 980 W ÷ 1300 W × 100 = 75.4%.
chapters.trap: Use the regulated output voltage and current for output power. Losses are input minus output. The regulator changes field current, not stator turns, to hold voltage.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5 for alternator construction and curves; basic power and efficiency.
chapters.leave: Detailed regulator integrated circuits to advanced electronics; battery sensing to Unit 3; charging circuit layout to Chapter 4.

chapters.idea: A starter must supply enough torque to crank a cold engine above its minimum starting speed despite compression, friction and battery voltage drop.
chapters.depth: Cover cranking torque, cranking speed and cranking power; effects of compression ratio, displacement, number of cylinders, oil viscosity and temperature; petrol versus diesel needs; battery voltage drop under high current. Use the starter torque-speed curve and engine resistance curve to explain the stable cranking point. Define angular speed ω = 2πN ÷ 60 and power P = Tω. Keep starter construction for Chapter 8.

figure.aria: Starter torque falls with speed while engine resistance rises; at 200 rpm the starter torque is 45 N·m.

chapters.example: A 4-cylinder petrol engine needs 45 N·m of cranking torque at 200 rpm. Find the cranking power. Answer: ω = 2πN ÷ 60 = 2π × 200 ÷ 60 = 20.94 rad/s; P = Tω = 45 N·m × 20.94 rad/s = 942 W.
chapters.trap: High compression, especially in a diesel, raises cranking torque. Starter power needs both torque and speed; a high torque at zero speed does no useful cranking work.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2 and 3 for battery cranking ability; basic four-stroke engine cycle.
chapters.leave: Starter motor types and drives to Chapter 8; ignition timing to Unit 2; engine friction details to engine courses.

chapters.idea: A starter motor uses a series or permanent-magnet DC motor, a drive that engages the flywheel, and a solenoid or relay that switches the very high current.
chapters.depth: Cover starter motor types: series-wound, permanent-magnet, gear-reduction and coaxial. Cover drives: Bendix inertia, pre-engaged, overrunning clutch and armature shift. Explain solenoid pull-in and hold-in coils, starter relay, ignition switch, terminal 30 (battery positive), terminal 50 (starter control) and terminal 15 (ignition). Draw the control and power circuit; include neutral or clutch safety switch and immobiliser interface. Keep battery CCA in Chapter 3.

figure.aria: A control sequence from driver key to ignition switch, relay, solenoid and starter shows a small control current switching the high starter current.

chapters.example: A starter draws 250 A at 10.5 V for 2.0 s. Find the charge used and the energy taken from the battery. Answer: Q = I t = 250 A × 2.0 s = 500 C, which is 500 ÷ 3600 = 0.139 Ah; P = V I = 10.5 V × 250 A = 2625 W; E = P t = 2625 W × 2.0 s = 5250 J.
chapters.trap: The ignition switch does not carry starter current; it operates a relay or solenoid. The solenoid has pull-in and hold-in coils, and the pinion must disengage after start.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7 for cranking torque and speed; Chapter 3 for battery CCA.
chapters.leave: Electronic start control and immobiliser details to Units 2 and 4; battery management to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Vehicle power distribution separates the 12 V bus from high-voltage ignition secondary and, in advanced study, EV traction high voltage, with fuses, relays and safety devices.
chapters.depth: Cover the 12 V backbone: battery positive, main fuse, fuse and relay box, ignition switch, wire gauge, voltage drop and chassis ground. Cover ignition secondary high voltage: coil, distributor or coil-on-plug, suppression leads and spark plug; keep spark generation and timing for Unit 2. Add EV traction high voltage only as advanced: about 400 V class, contactors, pre-charge, service disconnect, orange cable and isolation monitoring; say only a few universities teach this EV part. Do not mix the two voltage domains.

figure.aria: A distribution tree separates the 12 V bus, ignition secondary high voltage and, for advanced study, EV traction high voltage.

chapters.example: An ignition coil has a turns ratio of 100:1. The primary is interrupted at 350 V peak. Find the ideal secondary peak voltage. If the spark plug needs 8 kV to ionise the gap, find the voltage left to drive the arc in the secondary circuit. Answer: 350 V × 100 = 35,000 V = 35 kV; 35 kV − 8 kV = 27 kV.
chapters.trap: Do not mix ignition secondary kilovolts with EV traction hundreds of volts. A coil primary is low voltage, but the secondary is high voltage. A fuse protects wiring from excess current; it does not limit the spark voltage.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4 for the 12 V bus; Chapter 5 for rectified supply; basic electrical safety.
chapters.leave: Spark generation and ignition timing to Unit 2; EV battery management to Unit 3; vehicle networks to Unit 6.
